facts.what-is-history: Lesson facts to rely on: History is the study of people, places and events from the past; it helps us understand how life changed; historians ask who, what, where and why it mattered; evidence includes photographs, letters, memories, maps and objects; different evidence can show different points of view; use more than one source; Herodotus (c. 440 BCE) is called the Father of History; Ibn Khaldun wrote the Muqaddimah (1377)
facts.historical-sources: Lesson facts to rely on: A historical source is anything that gives information about the past; kinds are written (letter, diary, newspaper), visual (photograph, painting, map), oral (spoken memories, interviews, songs) and objects/artefacts (old cooking pot); primary source = from the time studied (diary, photograph); secondary source = made later using primary sources (textbook, documentary); ask who made a source, when, why, and whether other sources support it; writing began in Mesopotamia c. 3200 BCE; printing press c. 1450; practical photography 1839
facts.investigating-community: Lesson facts to rely on: A local history project investigates the history of your community; ask how people lived, worked, travelled, learned and celebrated; interview elders (oral evidence): ask permission before recording, prepare polite open questions, take notes; museums keep objects and displays; archives keep letters, photographs, maps, newspapers and records; old photographs show how places looked; compare interviews with other sources; District Six Museum, Cape Town, opened 1994
facts.timelines-change: Lesson facts to rely on: A timeline shows events in chronological order, earliest to latest; a decade is 10 years; a century is 100 years; BC = before AD 1, AD = after AD 1; in BC dates a bigger number is further back (500 BC is earlier than 100 BC); BCE = BC and CE = AD; timelines help show change over time; Julian calendar 45 BCE; Gregorian calendar 1582
facts.british-take-cape: Lesson facts to rely on: The Cape was a stop for fresh water, food and repairs on the sea route between Europe and India/the East; Dias rounded the Cape 1488; Jan van Riebeeck's Dutch station 1652; Britain first took the Cape from the Dutch in 1795; Britain took it again in 1806 (after Blaauwberg) and kept it for many years; British rule brought new laws, officials and settlers; slavery abolished at the Cape in 1834, but freedom did not mean immediate equality
facts.frontier-peoples: Lesson facts to rely on: Groups on the eastern frontier: Khoikhoi/San, Xhosa, Dutch/Boer Trekboers and later British settlers; Khoikhoi/San lived in southern Africa long before 1652; Xhosa farmed and kept cattle in the east; groups competed for land, water and cattle grazing; there was both cooperation (trade, working for one another, sharing skills) and conflict; colonial expansion caused unfairness; British arrived at the Cape 1795
facts.frontier-conflicts: Lesson facts to rely on: As the Cape Colony grew, settlers moved east into closer contact with the Xhosa; conflicts were about land, water, cattle and political power; raids, reprisals and unfair colonial policies made tension worse; the frontier wars were a series of conflicts over many years, mainly between settlers and the Xhosa; results were loss of life, loss of land and hardship; first frontier war 1779; sixth war 1834-1835; eighth war (War of Mlanjeni) 1850-1853; ninth war 1877-1879 was the last; study respectfully
facts.trekboers-migration: Lesson facts to rely on: Trekboers were Dutch-descended semi-nomadic farmers who moved inland from the Cape with families, wagons, cattle and sheep; they sought grazing and water, and some wanted independence from Cape officials; their movement affected Khoikhoi/San and Xhosa communities, leading to trade and cooperation but also conflict over land, water and grazing; Dutch station 1652; free burghers allowed beyond limits 1702; Great Trek 1830s grew out of this movement
facts.what-is-democracy: Lesson facts to rely on: Democracy means government by the people; adult citizens choose leaders by voting in free and fair elections; one person, one vote: each adult citizen's vote has equal value and people vote without being bullied or forced; under apartheid most South Africans were not allowed to vote; South Africa's first democratic election was on 27 April 1994, now Freedom Day; Nelson Mandela became the first democratically elected President; Athenian reforms 508/507 BCE; Magna Carta 1215
facts.road-to-democracy: Lesson facts to rely on: Under apartheid (a system of unfair separation and unequal rights) most South Africans could not vote in national elections; people worked for change through courage, negotiation and hope for peace; National Party began apartheid 1948; Freedom Charter adopted at Kliptown 1955; Mandela released 11 February 1990; Interim Constitution 1993; first democratic election 27 April 1994, celebrated as Freedom Day; Nelson Mandela became the first democratically elected President; long voting queues
facts.constitution-bill-rights: Lesson facts to rely on: The Constitution is the highest law of South Africa; all other laws and government actions must follow it; the Bill of Rights is part of the Constitution and protects everyone, including equality, dignity, education, safety and freedom; people must respect the rights of others; apartheid began 1948; Freedom Charter 1955; Interim Constitution 1993; first democratic election 1994; final Constitution came into force 4 February 1997
facts.rights-responsibilities: Lesson facts to rely on: In a democracy citizens have rights and responsibilities; example right: education; example responsibilities: respect teachers and classmates, respect other people's rights and freedom; responsibilities help protect everyone's rights; South Africa has three levels (spheres) of government: national (whole country), provincial (a province) and local or municipal; the Constitution set out these spheres (1996); first all-adult national vote 1994; new municipalities began 2000
facts.ancient-medicine: Lesson facts to rely on: Ancient healers used herbs, simple tools, bandages and careful observation; they often did not know what caused disease and blamed bad air, angry gods, spirits or an imbalance in the body; this was before germ theory; Egyptians, Greeks, Romans, Chinese, Indian and African societies all developed medical ideas; some ideas were wrong but healers helped by cleaning wounds and using plant remedies; knowledge grew by asking questions and testing ideas; Imhotep c. 2600 BCE; Ebers Papyrus c. 1550 BCE; Hippocrates c. 400 BCE; Galen c. 200 CE
facts.early-indigenous-medicine: Lesson facts to rely on: Long ago people healed with plants, herbs, roots, bark and other natural remedies; in South Africa an inyanga is often a herbalist who uses medicinal plants; a sangoma is often a diviner and spiritual healer; this is part of indigenous knowledge systems; knowledge was learned by observing nature, listening to elders and practising, and passed down generation to generation; study it with respect; Traditional Health Practitioners Act 2007 recognised traditional healers
facts.european-medicine: Lesson facts to rely on: More hospitals were built where the sick were cared for and medical workers learned; germ theory: tiny germs cause disease, so cleanliness, handwashing, clean water and hygienic hospitals matter; vaccines train the body to fight certain diseases before a person becomes seriously sick; early hospitals c. 370 CE; Jenner's smallpox vaccine 1796; Semmelweis handwashing 1847; Pasteur and germ theory 1861; Lister's antiseptic surgery 1867
facts.modern-medicine: Lesson facts to rely on: Modern medicine uses X-rays, stethoscopes, tests and medicines to diagnose and treat illness; antibiotics kill or stop many bacteria (not every illness) and should be used only when prescribed; penicillin was one of the first widely used antibiotics; X-rays discovered 1895 (Rontgen); penicillin found 1928 (Fleming), widely used 1943; Dr Christiaan Barnard performed the first human heart transplant in Cape Town, South Africa, in 1967
facts.gr6-limpopo-valley-k2-schroda-t1: Lesson facts to rely on: between about AD 900 and AD 1300 the societies of the Limpopo Valley became bigger, more organised and more complex; Schroda was a farming settlement about AD 900 to 1000 (about 100 years) where people kept cattle, made pottery and had ivory and glass beads that show trade with far away people; K2 was a bigger settlement about AD 1000 to 1220 (about 220 years) where cattle were a sign of wealth and leaders became more important; the people moved to Mapungubwe Hill about AD 1220; Mapungubwe lasted from AD 1220 to AD 1300 (80 years); the whole story covers 400 years; archaeologists study objects and remains left by people of the past; cattle, farming and trade stayed important (continuity) while settlements grew (change). Use 'about' for the dates of Schroda and K2.
facts.gr6-mapungubwe-kingdom-t1: Lesson facts to rely on: Mapungubwe was the first state in southern Africa, from AD 1220 to AD 1300 (80 years), ruled by a king who was a sacred leader (people believed he had special sacred powers); the king and leaders lived on top of Mapungubwe Hill and were buried there; the palace on the hill was the first stone-walled palace in southern Africa; the first town grew below the hill, with farmers, herders, potters and metalworkers; there were distinct social classes (the king and leaders, and the ordinary people), shown by where people lived and by graves with gold on the hill; the people came from the earlier settlement of K2; Mapungubwe was built by the people of southern Africa.
facts.gr6-mapungubwe-trade-today-t1: Lesson facts to rely on: a small golden rhinoceros, a golden bowl and a golden sceptre were found in royal graves on Mapungubwe Hill in the 1930s and were symbols of royal power and political leadership; Mapungubwe traded gold and ivory and received glass beads and cloth, across Africa and across the Indian Ocean (globalisation means places far apart joined by trade); traders walked to the east coast, with dangers such as wild animals, lack of water and getting lost, and found their way by landmarks such as hills and rivers, the sun and stars and local guides; today the Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape is a World Heritage Site (named in 2003) and the Order of Mapungubwe is a South African honour (created in 2002).
